candidates.attacker_control: The remote address evaluated by the check (`getMessageContext().getHttpServletRequest().getRemoteAddr()`) is the source address of whoever sends the HTTP request, and the access token is supplied by the caller in the `Authorization` header. The registered `clientIpAddress` is server-side configuration, but the inverted comparison means requests from any address other than that one pass the check, so an attacker outside the intended network origin is accepted.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: I considered that `clientIpAddress` might be intended as a deny-list, but that is implausible from the field name/API (`Client.getClientIpAddress`), the fact that it is copied into `AccessTokenValidation` as the token's client attribute, and the thrown message "Client IP Address is invalid" — all consistent with reject-on-mismatch. I checked for another enforcement point that could compensate: repo-wide search for `ClientIpAddress`/`setClientIpAddress` shows this filter is the only consumer, so nothing else enforces the binding. I noted that `getRemoteAddr()` may return a proxy address, but that does not alter the inverted logic. I verified the filter is a public `@Provider` and is also subclassed as `OAuthRequestInterceptor` (an interceptor-chain entry), so it is a real enforcement path when configured.
candidates.impact: Authorization bypass of the OAuth2 client IP-address restriction: an access token minted for an IP-bound client can be used from an arbitrary network location (for example an attacker host), defeating a defense-in-depth control whose stated purpose is to bind token use to the client's address. The same inversion also causes a denial of service for the legitimate client when it calls from its registered IP. Confidentiality and integrity of the OAuth2-protected endpoints are affected once such a token is obtained.
candidates.prerequisites: An application whose JAX-RS/JAX-WS endpoints are protected with CXF's OAuth2 `OAuthRequestFilter`/`OAuthRequestInterceptor` and whose `OAuthDataProvider` returns clients/tokens carrying a `clientIpAddress` (i.e., the client IP-binding feature is in use). The caller must present an access token issued for such a client (for example a token obtained or leaked through logs, redirects or a compromised client). No additional privileges are needed to originate a request from a different IP.
candidates.root_cause: In `OAuthRequestFilter.validateRequest(...)`, the check intended to restrict an access token to the client's registered IP address is inverted: it throws 403 when the request's remote address *equals* the registered client IP (`accessTokenV.getClientIpAddress().equals(remoteAddress)`) and therefore admits the request when the address differs. The correct predicate is `!equals`. Because the security control fails open, it provides no protection and simultaneously blocks legitimate use from the allowed address.
candidates.title: Inverted client-IP comparison in OAuthRequestFilter defeats OAuth2 client IP binding
candidates.trace: Inbound request -> `OAuthRequestFilter.filter` -> `validateRequest(m)` -> `getAccessTokenValidation(...)` builds `AccessTokenValidation` from the token, copying `token.getClient().getClientIpAddress()` (AccessTokenValidation.java:57-61) -> lines 122-128 evaluate `remoteAddress == null || clientIpAddress.equals(remoteAddress)`. If the source IP matches the registered IP the request is rejected with 403 ("Client IP Address is invalid"); if it does not match, execution continues to the scope/verb checks and the protected resource is served.
candidates.unverified: Runtime confirmation was not performed (no code executed). Whether the dataset's intended target is this specific defect is not established; the finding is based on source evidence. Whether a given deployment registers clients with `clientIpAddress` (the vulnerable control is optional/configuration-dependent) was not verified, and behaviour behind reverse proxies (`getRemoteAddr` returning a proxy IP) was not tested.

coverage_summary: Snapshot = Apache CXF 3.0.11 tree: 4,350 files (3,528 Java, ~22.5 MB), all `src/test` sources stripped. P1 relation index is partial: 4,299 files indexed, 51 source files missing from the index, 5 parse errors, and no control-flow/data-flow or semantic resolution (syntactic call/inheritance/containment candidates only, ~96k unresolved calls); index labels were used purely for navigation and every cited location was verified in source text. I reviewed the HTTP transport/servlet stack (servlet controller, service-list writers, CORS, TLS/JSSE helpers, Netty/Jetty destinations), JAX-RS frontend and body providers (XMLSource, SourceProvider, XPath/JAXB/DOM4J/XMLBeans/XSLT providers, RequestPreprocessor), JOSE/JWT/JWS/JWE, OAuth 1.0 and OAuth2 (filters, grant handlers, redirection services, data providers), SAML/OIDC SSO, WS-Security/STS schema download, management-web Atom/log code, and selected core utilities (StaxUtils, Compiler, TunedDocumentLoader). Large areas were only sampled: CORBA/JMS/JCA transports, WS-RM/WS-Policy/WS-Addressing, OSGi/blueprint wiring, code-generation tools, and the bundled samples/benchmarks.
limitations: Static source review only: no code was compiled, executed or fuzzed, and no exploit payloads were used; reachability and impact are based on source reading.
No test trees exist in the snapshot, so fix/regression behaviour could not be inferred from tests.

The relation index is explicitly partial (51 source files unindexed, 5 parse errors) and lacks control/data-flow and semantic resolution; unindexed/unparsed files cannot be treated as reviewed via the index.
Whether the specific candidate matches the benchmark's underlying CVE/fix commit is inferred, not confirmed; no external CVE, patch or ground-truth data was consulted.
The client-IP binding is an optional OAuth2 feature, so real-world exploitability depends on deployment configuration that is not present in this snapshot.
No runtime validation of `getRemoteAddr()` behaviour behind proxies/load balancers was possible.

rejected_leads.lead: Blind SSRF via `JwtRequestCodeFilter.process` (`request_uri` parameter) — `isRequestUriValid` only checks `startsWith("https://")` (with a TODO about restricting hosts) before `WebClient.create(requestUri).get(String.class)`.
rejected_leads.reason: Real weakness, but it is an optional `AuthorizationCodeRequestFilter` that must be configured, requires an authenticated OAuth client, and the fetched content must still pass JWT signature/decryption verification, making it a blind SSRF with weaker evidence than the submitted candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Unencoded request URI / Host reflected into the services page (`FormattedServiceListWriter` lines 55, 58, 112-118, 162-165; `ServiceListGeneratorServlet` line 116 builds the stylesheet path from `request.getRequestURI()`).
rejected_leads.reason: No HTML escaping is applied, but browser URI encoding of `<`, `>` and `"` and container normalization make a browser-executable XSS uncertain from source alone; impact is also limited to deployments exposing the service list page. Unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: Setter typo in `AbstractOAuthJoseJwtConsumer.setDecryptWithClientSecret` (lines 61-63) assigns `decryptWithClientSecret = verifyWithClientSecret`, ignoring the parameter.
rejected_leads.reason: Silently leaves JWE decryption disabled (JWE-only configurations fail), which looks like an availability/configuration defect rather than an authentication bypass; no path was found where it weakens a successful verification decision.

rejected_leads.lead: CORS filter reflects any `Origin` when `allowCredentials` is enabled with default (empty) allow-origins (`CrossOriginResourceSharingFilter` lines 323-339).
rejected_leads.reason: Configuration-dependent design choice rather than an unconditional flaw; not chosen as the single candidate.

The class already creates DOMs through `StaxUtils` (core `StaxUtils.createXMLInputFactory`, lines 307-351, disables DTDs, entity replacement and external entities and installs a blocking XMLResolver), so no XXE path was found. The remaining `DocumentBuilderFactory` usages (`AbstractSTSClient.downloadSchema` sets `disallow-doctype-decl`; Aegis `XMLTypeCreator.readAegisFile` parses local `.aegis.xml` mapping files) were likewise not attacker-reachable from request data.

rejected_leads.lead: Header/method overrides in `RequestPreprocessor` (`_method`, `X-HTTP-Method-Override`) and CRLF/redirect handling in `AbstractHTTPServlet`.
rejected_leads.reason: Investigated; no concrete cross-boundary bypass could be established from source without knowing the consuming application's authorization model.

summary: Scope analyzed: Apache CXF snapshot at the 3.0.11 release state (root pom `3.0.11`, release notes 3.0.11), 4,350 source files / 3,528 Java files, with all `src/test` sources absent. I surveyed the HTTP transport/servlet layer, JAX-RS frontend and providers, JOSE/JWT, OAuth 1.0/2.0, SAML/OIDC, WS-Security/STS, XML parsing utilities, and management-web. The strongest verifiable security defect is an inverted authorization comparison in the OAuth2 resource-server filter: an access token bound to a client IP address is accepted from every address except the bound one, so the IP restriction fails open (and the legitimate client is denied). Static review only; no code was executed.
